lesson.title: What is Coding? Meet Python
lesson.description: Learn what coding and programming languages are, meet Python and write your first line of code: print("Hello World!").

blocks.title: Talking to computers
blocks.text:
Computers are fast, but they can't think for themselves. They only do exactly what they are told.

**Coding** (also called **programming**) is writing step-by-step instructions that a computer can follow. A set of instructions that does a job is called a **program**: every app, game and website you use is a program.

## Like a recipe
A recipe tells a cook what to do, in order:
1. Crack two eggs into a bowl
2. Whisk them
3. Pour them into a hot pan

Code works the same way, except the cook is a computer, and it follows every step *exactly* as written. If a step is unclear or in the wrong order, the result is wrong too.

> Deep down, computers only understand **binary**: long strings of 0s and 1s. Nobody wants to write that by hand, which is why we use programming languages.

blocks.title: Why so many languages?
blocks.text:
A **programming language** is a way of writing instructions that both people and computers can understand. A special tool then translates your code into the 0s and 1s the computer runs.

There are hundreds of languages because different jobs need different tools, just like a builder uses a hammer for nails and a saw for wood. Some languages are best for websites, some for games, some for phone apps and some for analysing data.

## High-level vs low-level
- **Low-level** languages are close to how the computer's hardware works. They are very fast, but hard for people to read.
- **High-level** languages read more like English. They are much easier to learn and write, which makes them great for beginners.

Python is a **high-level** language.

items.title: Low-level languages
items.text: Close to the hardware. **Machine code** is pure binary; **assembly** uses short codes like `MOV` and `ADD`. Used where every bit of speed matters.

items.title: High-level languages
items.text: Written in words people can read, such as Python, JavaScript and Java. Most programmers work with these.

items.title: Compiled languages
items.text: The whole program is translated into machine code *before* it runs, so it usually runs very fast. Examples: C, C++, Rust, Go.

items.title: Interpreted languages
items.text: The code is translated and run *step by step* by a program called an interpreter, so you can try things quickly. Examples: Python, JavaScript, Ruby.

items.title: Markup and styling languages
items.text: HTML describes the structure of a web page and CSS describes how it looks. They don't give step-by-step instructions, so they aren't usually called programming languages, but you'll use them often.

items.title: Query languages
items.text: SQL is used to ask databases questions, like *show me every student older than 12*.

blocks.title: What is Python?
blocks.text:
**Python** is a high-level, general-purpose programming language. *General-purpose* means you can use it for almost anything: websites, games, robots, data and artificial intelligence.

Python is famous for being **easy to read**. Compare how two languages show the same message.

Java:
```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello World!");
    }
}
```
Python:
```python
print("Hello World!")
```
## Why people love Python
- Short, clean code that looks a lot like English
- Free to use, and runs on Windows, macOS and Linux
- Huge collection of ready-made tools, called **libraries**
- A large, friendly community, so help is easy to find
- Used by beginners *and* by big companies

items.title: 1989: An idea over the holidays
items.text: Dutch programmer **Guido van Rossum** started building Python as a hobby project during his Christmas holidays, while working at the CWI research institute in the Netherlands.

items.title: The name
items.text: Python is *not* named after the snake. Guido was a fan of the British comedy show **Monty Python's Flying Circus** and wanted a short, slightly mysterious name.

items.title: 1991: First release
items.text: Python 0.9.0 was shared publicly in February 1991, so anyone could use it.

items.title: 2000: Python 2
items.text: Python 2.0 added popular features and Python's community grew quickly.

items.title: 2008: Python 3
items.text: Python 3.0 cleaned up the language. It wasn't fully compatible with Python 2, so moving over took the community years.

items.title: 2020: Goodbye, Python 2
items.text: Support for Python 2 officially ended on 1 January 2020. Today everyone uses **Python 3**, and so will you.

items.title: Today
items.text: Python is one of the most popular programming languages in the world, and one of the most common first languages taught in schools.

items.title: Building websites
items.text: Python runs the *behind-the-scenes* part of many websites, such as logins and saving data. Popular tools include **Django** and **Flask**, and Instagram is a well-known site built with Django.

items.title: Data science and AI
items.text: Scientists and companies use Python to analyse huge amounts of data and to build artificial intelligence. Libraries such as **pandas**, **NumPy** and **PyTorch** make this much easier.

items.title: Automating boring tasks
items.text: Python scripts can rename hundreds of files, fill in spreadsheets or send reminders, saving hours of repetitive work.

items.title: Games, robots and gadgets
items.text: You can make games with **Pygame**, and Python runs on small computers like the **Raspberry Pi** to control robots, lights and sensors.

blocks.title: Hello, World!
blocks.text:
It's tradition: the first program most people write simply shows the words **Hello World!** on the screen. The tradition was made famous by the 1978 book *The C Programming Language*, and programmers have kept it going ever since.

In Python, it takes just one line:
```python
print("Hello World!")
```
When you run it, Python shows this **output**:
```
Hello World!
```
## What is a function?
`print` is a **function**: a ready-made command that does a job for you. You *call* a function by writing its name followed by brackets `()`. Whatever you put inside the brackets is passed to the function. `print()` shows it on the screen.

items.title: print
items.text: The name of the function. It must be all **lowercase**: `Print` won't work.
Brackets (also called parentheses) hold what you give to the function. Every `(` needs a matching `)`.
Quotation marks show that this is **text**, called a **string**. You can use double `"` or single `'` quotes, but the start and end must match.

items.title: Hello World!
items.text: The text you want to show. It can be anything you like: `print("I love coding!")`

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
Python is very strict about **syntax** (its grammar). These small slips cause errors:

```python
Print("Hello World!")    # capital P -> NameError
print(Hello World!)      # no quotes -> SyntaxError
print("Hello World!"     # missing ) -> SyntaxError
print("Hello World!')    # quotes don't match -> SyntaxError
```
Errors are normal! Every programmer sees them all the time. Read the error message: it usually tells you which line to check.

> **Tip:** Lines starting with `#` are **comments**. Python ignores them, so they're handy for notes to yourself.
